newsitem.title: INDIA: India urges speeding up South Asian free trade.
newsitem.headline: India urges speeding up South Asian free trade.

text.p: South Asian foreign ministers began a two-day meeting on Thursday with a call from India to strengthen economic cooperation and speed up moves towards regional free trade.

"When we are deregulating our economies and opening our markets to the world, inviting global competition, it stands to reason that we should join forces and enhance our collective strength, range and dynamism," Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told the ministers from seven nations.
Inaugurating a ministerial meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), Deve Gowda said there was encouraging progress in building economic ties.

SAARC is comprised of the Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal, the Indian Ocean island republics of Maldives and Sri Lanka, mostly Hindu India and its Moslem majority neighbours, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Many of its 1.2 billion people live in dire poverty and would benefit from economic growth spurred by increased trade.
Earlier this year SAARC commerce ministers agreed to try to establish a South Asia Free Trade Area (SAPTA) by 2000.
Last month, SAARC member countries agreed to reduce tariffs on more than 1,500 products, up from 226 items covered in the first round of talks ended one year ago.

Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said SAARC could move faster towards free trade. Last month Deve Gowda inaugurated a conference of leading industrialists which endorsed setting a target date of 1998 for free trade.
"In the future we will need to move much faster and no doubt impetus will be added as we proceed," Gujral said.
He urged the ministers to call for the immediate start of a third round of trade talks.

The meeting, preceded by a gathering of foreign secretaries earlier this week, was the 11-year-old group's first following landmark agreements ending disputes between India and neighbours Bangladesh and Nepal.
Both accords concerned water-sharing, a crucial issue in the subcontinent where most people still depend on agriculture for a living. The accords have opened up new vistas for cooperation.
But trade between SAARC countries accounts for only three percent of the nations' total trade, and some 4,500 products remain untouched.
Uneasy ties between India and Pakistan have overshadowed SAARC's efforts for a free trade bloc.
India is by far the most populous member state and has offered about half of the trade concessions. But it has failed to win most favoured nation (MFN) trade status from arch-rival Pakistan.

India has already granted MFN status -- under which two countries undertake to give each other the maximum tariff concessions on their mutual trade which they already grant to other countries -- to all SAARC nations, including Pakistan.
